title: The Cabuliwallah
subtitle: Rabindranath Tagore (1892) — a fruit-seller from Kabul, a five-year-old in Calcutta, and a handprint on a piece of paper.
crosslink: Need an easier version? Read this story at A2/B1 level →
grammar_tab: Grammar — Past Habits: used to, would, be used to
intention: you'll tell a story about two fathers and a friendship across a great distance, and use used to, would and be used to to talk about how things were and how people change.
warmup: Think of a grown-up who was kind to you when you were small — not a relative. What do you remember about them?
Who counts as a stranger? At what point does a stranger stop being one?
Is it ever right to let a child make friends with someone the family doesn't quite trust?
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's unlock the words you'll need. Think first — the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A. Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: A pedlar came down the street every winter with a bag on his back and boxes of grapes in his hands, calling at each house in turn.
items.meaning: a pedlar (n) — someone who travels from place to place selling small goods. (Also spelt peddler.)

items.sent: She was so timid that a knock at the door could make her hide, and every noise in the street was a thief or a tiger.
items.meaning: timid (adj) — easily frightened; lacking courage or confidence.

items.sent: He looked at me wistfully, said good morning, and went out — a man who had hoped for something and been refused.
items.meaning: wistfully (adv) — with a quiet, sad longing for something you cannot have.

items.sent: Having given the money away, I had to curtail the celebrations: no electric lights, no military band.
items.meaning: to curtail (v) — to reduce or cut short.

vocab.heading: B. Close in meaning, or opposite?
vocab.instruction: Say the word that fits, then reveal.

items.sent: Vexed is close in meaning to which everyday word — annoyed, bored, or excited?
items.meaning: vexed (adj) ≈ annoyed, irritated. Her mother is often vexed at her chatter.

items.sent: Precarious is the opposite of which word — secure, expensive, or slow?
items.meaning: precarious (adj) — the opposite of secure: dangerously uncertain, likely to fall or fail.

items.sent: Judicious is close in meaning to which word — wise, quick, or generous?
items.meaning: judicious (adj) ≈ wise, showing good judgement. a judicious bribery of nuts and almonds

vocab.heading: C. Choose the meaning
vocab.instruction: One sentence, three options. Say a, b or c — then reveal.

items.sent: Among his people, 'the father-in-law's house' was a euphemism for prison. A euphemism is: (a) a rude word for something (b) a mild or indirect word used instead of an unpleasant one (c) a word from another language
items.meaning: (b) — a euphemism (n) is a gentler or indirect expression used in place of a blunt one.

items.sent: He looked staggered when the young bride walked in. Staggered means: (a) delighted (b) bored (c) shocked and unsteady with surprise
items.meaning: (c) — staggered (adj) — so surprised that you can hardly stand or speak.

items.sent: She stood bashfully before him, her face turned down. Bashfully means: (a) shyly, with embarrassment (b) angrily (c) proudly

vocab_use: Put the ten words into three groups: words about people and character, words about feelings, and words about situations. Say why.
Using pedlar, timid and euphemism, predict what kind of story this is.
story_intro: Tagore's story in the 1916 English translation, lightly shortened. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

story.title: Part 1 — A man with a bag

paras.from: My five years' old daughter Mini

check.q: Why does Mini run away from the Cabuliwallah the first time she sees him?
check.a: She has a 'blind belief' that the big man's bag contains two or three other children like herself.

check.q: What does the father do about her fear, and does it work?
check.a: He has her brought out to meet the man; the pedlar offers nuts and raisins, but she refuses them and clings closer to her father, with 'all her doubts increased'.

story.discuss: The father is writing a romantic adventure novel while a real adventure walks past his window. What does Tagore want us to notice about him?

story.title: Part 2 — 'What have you got in your bag?'

paras.from: One morning, however, not many days later
skip: proceeded to make my own inquiries.
I could see the string of camels

check.q: What are the two jokes that Mini and Rahmun share, and what does 'the father-in-law's house' mean to each of them?
check.a: 'What have you got in your bag?' — 'An elephant!'; and 'When are you going to the father-in-law's house?' To Mini it is a puzzling question about marriage; to Rahmun and his people it is a euphemism for prison.

check.q: Why does the mother distrust the pedlar, and why does the father let the friendship go on?
check.a: She fears kidnapping and slavery in Kabul — she is timid about everything. The father thinks it 'highly improbable' and, since the fear is indefinite, sees no right to forbid the man the house.

story.discuss: The father dreams of mountains and camels whenever he sees a foreigner; the mother sees thieves and tigers. Which of them is closer to how most people react to strangers?

story.title: Part 3 — Eight years

paras.from: One morning, a few days before he had made up his mind
paras.to: met again with his only child.
skip: From early morning noise and bustle

check.q: Why is Rahmun arrested, and what is the last thing he says to Mini before prison?
check.a: A neighbour refuses to pay for a shawl, they quarrel, and Rahmun strikes him. Holding up his bound hands he tells Mini he would have thrashed the 'father-in-law' but his hands are tied — and that prison is 'just where I am going'.

check.q: What is on the piece of paper, and what does it change?
check.a: The ink-print of his own small daughter's hand, carried against his heart for years. It makes the father see that Rahmun is a father too — 'what was I more than he?' — and he sends for Mini, and then gives Rahmun money to go home.

story.discuss: The father pays for Rahmun's journey by cancelling the lights and the band at his daughter's wedding. Was that generosity, guilt, or something else?

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: how things used to be
grammar.intro: This is a story about habits that end. A pedlar used to come every winter; a little girl would run to the window; eight years later nobody is used to him any more. English has three tools here, and learners mix them up constantly.
notes:
1. used to + verb — a past habit or state that has now stopped.
• "My grandfather used to smoke a pipe." (habit) • "There used to be a cinema here." (state)
• Negative and question: "He didn't use to like coffee." / "Did you use to play chess?"

2. would + verb — repeated past actions, often in storytelling.
• "Every summer we would drive to the coast and my father would complain about the traffic."
• Only for actions, never for states: ✗ would be tall, ✗ would have a car. If in doubt, used to is always safe.

3. be / get used to + -ing (or a noun) — accustomed to something.
• "She is used to working nights." (it's normal for her now) • "You'll get used to the noise." (become accustomed)
This one is about the present or a process — nothing to do with past habits, despite the spelling.

exercises.h3: used to, didn't use to, did… use to — and where would fits
exercises.instruction: Complete each sentence. Where the hint says (would), use would; otherwise use a form of used to.
items: ___ Mini ___ (talk) to the pedlar every morning? — Yes, for weeks.
Her mother ___ (not / trust) strangers — and she still doesn't.
Rahmun ___ (have) long hair and a bag on his back.
Every autumn the Cabuliwallah ___ (return / would) to his mountains.
exercises.note: 3 is a state (have), so would is impossible there.

exercises.h3: used to + verb, or be / get used to + -ing?
exercises.instruction: Follow the hint: (be) or (get) means the accustomed sense with -ing; a bare verb means a past habit.
items: Mini ___ (not / be / see) strangers at the door, so she ran to her mother.
Rahmun ___ (sell) fruit in these streets every winter, before prison.
In prison he slowly ___ (get / live) without the mountains.
"You'll soon ___ (get / her) chatter," the father said.
She ___ (be) a talkative child; she is quiet and shy now.

exercises.h3: Put it together — eight years in one paragraph
exercises.instruction: Fill each gap with used to, would or was/were used to and the verb given. Read it aloud when you've finished.
items: When Mini was five she ___ (run) to the window every time she heard his voice, and the two of them ___ (laugh) at the same two jokes for hours. Her father ___ (dream) of mountains whenever the pedlar came; her mother never ___ (get / him). Eight years later, Rahmun was still not ___ (be / think) of Mini as anything but a child — and the child ___ (not / be) a child any more.
answers: would run (used to run) · would laugh (used to laugh) · would dream (used to dream) · got used to him · used to thinking · didn't use to be — or, more naturally, was no longer
exercises.note: Where an action repeats in a story, would sounds most natural; used to is never wrong.

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab you'll narrate the friendship with would, mark what has ended with used to, and describe what people are and aren't accustomed to with be used to.

deeper.h2: Why this story stays with you
paras: Rabindranath Tagore wrote 'The Cabuliwallah' in Bengali in 1892, when Calcutta was the capital of British India and Afghan traders — Kabuliwalas, 'men from Kabul' — walked its streets every winter selling dried fruit and lending money. In 1913 he became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize for Literature; this English version appeared in 1916, in a collection Tagore oversaw himself.

The story is told by a comfortable man who thinks he is watching a charming friendship between his daughter and a poor stranger. Only at the very end does he understand what he has been watching: another father, with another daughter, carrying her handprint against his heart for eight years. The whole story turns on one sentence — 'what was I more than he?' — and on what the narrator does next. He sends for Mini, and he gives away the wedding lights. Tagore does not tell us whether that is enough.
deeper.note: Look again at the handprint. 'Not a photograph. Not a drawing.' Why does Tagore insist on this? What can a print of a hand do that a photograph cannot?
questions: The narrator admits his 'heart shrank' when he learned Rahmun had been in prison, and that he wished the man had not come. How honest is this narrator about himself — and does his honesty make him easier or harder to forgive?
Mini, at thirteen, cannot answer the old joke; she blushes and looks down. What has she lost, and what has she gained? Is growing up always a kind of forgetting?
The story is called 'The Cabuliwallah', but it is really about the narrator. Or is it about the mother, whose fears turn out to be half right — Rahmun did have a knife? Who is the story about?
Two fathers, one rich, one poor, one Bengali, one Afghan. Tagore was writing under an empire that divided people by race and rank. What is the story quietly arguing?

speak.useful: Tell the habit years with would and used to: "Every morning he would…", "She used to run to the window…", "They didn't use to…"; the change with be / get used to: "He wasn't used to seeing her as…". For opinions: "What's striking is…", "You could argue that…", "On one level… but on another…".

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the whole story (4 minutes)
paras: Tell 'The Cabuliwallah' to someone who has never read it. Move through the arc: the man at the window → the friendship and the two jokes → the mother's fears → the arrest → eight years later, the wedding morning → the handprint → the money and the cancelled band.
Use used to, would and be used to deliberately, and at least five key words (pedlar, timid, wistfully, curtail, vexed, precarious, judicious, euphemism, staggered, bashfully).

tasks.label: Task B · 'What was I more than he?' (4 minutes)
paras: The narrator decides that he and the Afghan pedlar are equals — as fathers. Then he gives him a banknote and sends him away. Build an argument: does the ending show real equality, or does it show a rich man buying back his good opinion of himself? Then argue the other side for one minute.

tasks.label: Task C · Someone who came back (4 minutes)
paras: Tell a story — real, famous or invented — about someone who returns after years away and finds that everything they knew has changed. Use used to and would for how things were, and be / get used to for what they now have to accept.
menu: A migrant worker who comes home after a decade and meets children who barely remember him.
A prisoner released after a long sentence, standing outside a house that used to be his.
A soldier back from a war that the people at home have already stopped talking about.
Rip Van Winkle, who sleeps for twenty years and wakes into a different country.
A childhood friend you meet again as an adult — and the jokes that no longer work.
A teacher who taught you when you were small, met years later in the street.

final: The mother's fears were 'highly improbable' — and Rahmun did turn out to carry a knife. Were her fears foolish, or was the father naïve?
Is a friendship between a five-year-old and a grown stranger something to encourage or to worry about — in 1892, and now?
The narrator gives up the electric lights and the band. What would you have given up — and would you have sent for Mini?
Before you go — from memory: one sentence with used to, one with would, one with be used to — and tell me which of the three can't be used for a state like have or be.
